title: The Mystery of 8,000 Ancient Frogs — Solved by Owls
summary:
It was a cold case 1,700 years old: 8,000 dead frogs piled into a ditch in Cambridgeshire, England. Scientists have solved the mystery — the frogs were a feast for hungry owls.

The bones turned up between 2016 and 2018, during highway work. Radiocarbon dating placed the frogs in the Roman era. Measuring the frogs' arm bones showed most had died young, eaten in the winter of their first year. The ditch had filled within a single year.

Zooarchaeologist Paul Clarkson of Bournemouth University studied the damage on the bones and concluded that birds of prey had eaten the frogs. Short-eared owls were the most likely hunters, though hen harriers were also suspects. The bones may be leftovers from a whole community of predators, which also fed on shrews, mice, and voles.

Why so many frogs in one place? As the wetlands around the ditch dried out, the area became breeding ground for frogs. People had also cleared woodland for grazing land, leaving the frogs with less cover. The cleared land suited short-eared owls, which hunt over open grassland.
why_it_matters: Old bones can tell a story, just like clues in a mystery book, and learning to read them helps you solve puzzles in the world around you.

background_read: Long ago, the land in this part of England was wet marshland, a good home for frogs.
When animals die, their bones can stay in the ground for a very long time, and scientists can study the marks on them to learn what ate them.
Owls and other birds of prey hunt small animals, and the leftovers from their meals can pile up in one place over time.
